title: A National Viral Radar for a Global Mass Gathering

# A National Viral Radar for a Global Mass Gathering


### Review of the Biobot World Cup Wastewater Metagenomics Program


[Mariana Matus](https://substack.com/@marianamatus)


and[Josh Harrison](https://substack.com/@harrisonjg)


Oct 30, 2026


Last summer, millions of people crossed oceans, countries, and state lines to watch soccer. The World Cup coincided with the United States’ 250th anniversary events, an international naval review, and summer travel season. Meanwhile, one of the largest Ebola outbreaks on record was unfolding in the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Andes hantavirus cluster was tied to a cruise ship, and one of the biggest foodborne outbreaks in US history was spreading, largely unseen by routine testing.


A mass gathering doesn’t create an outbreak on its own. But it makes introductions more likely, and it asks a hard question of every surveillance system: would you see it?


We wanted to find out. So we ran the experiment.


**From “Is it there?” to “What is there?”**


Biobot started with a simple idea: sewage is a public health observatory that already exists. We were the first to detect SARS-CoV-2 in US wastewater in early 2020, and we’ve since expanded to opioids, dozens of pathogens, and hundreds of communities across the nation.


Most of that work, like most of public health surveillance, rests on targeted PCR. It is sensitive and precise, but it only answers the question you thought to ask. You choose the virus before you look. You remain ignorant to the illnesses you choose not to look for, though they are present nevertheless.


Metagenomics flips the question. Instead of asking whether virus X is circulating, it asks what all the viruses circulating are. For the World Cup, together with the Maresso and Tisza labs at Baylor College of Medicine, we ran hybrid capture sequencing on a panel designed to capture more than 3,000 viruses. Baylor has refined this approach for over six years. For the past five years, they have used this assay in eleven Texan municipal areas. It has proven invaluable for local public health. For instance, the assay caught H5N1 across ten cities and, and measles in Houston in early 2025.


We scaled this assay to monitor 14 sentinel sites representing roughly 14 million people in areas associated with soccer matches and large urban hubs. Participating sites sampled weekly for ten weeks, totalling 579 samples sequenced. For more details on the method, including peer-reviewed publications see our


[World Cup dashboard](https://biobotworldcup2026.com/virome-metagenomics) .


**What the radar saw**


Most of what we found was ordinary, and that is a feature, not a disappointment. We identified 983 viral species, 133 of them relevant to human health (Fig. 1).


Fig. 1 Viral species of known relevance to human health summarized by viral family. Many of these viruses are typically untracked but can cause a disease burden.


We saw the summer SARS-CoV-2 wave build, and in Houston the wastewater signal tracked emergency department visits closely (Spearman correlation of 0.88; Fig. 2).


Fig. 2 The SARS-CoV-2 summer wave found in wastewater (top panel) matched the wave reported by emergency departments (bottom panel).


We also saw the everyday viruses that make people sick but rarely get tested for: GI infections, rhinovirus, parainfluenza and others. Routine surveillance has real gaps, and metagenomics fills them.


We detected measles in places with and without reported cases. We resolved mpox to clade I and clade II from sequence data alone, which matters enormously for a public health response. And we found zero high consequence pathogens (Ebola, Marburg, and the like), which was a reassuring result for a summer like this one.


**The signal that became our deepest investigation: rubella**


In a routine sample, we saw rubella reads. We double checked the bioinformatic analysis, and it persisted at one site and appeared nowhere else. Viral concentration stayed flat over time, where a true infection with ongoing transmission would be expected to grow or fade. When we compared the sequence to available genomes, it matched a vaccine or vector derived strain.


We notified local and federal partners about the detections. Multiple genomic scientists reviewed the data independently. Every line of evidence pointed the same way: the most likely source was a research facility, not an infection. In fact, a quick online search revealed that there was a facility that makes rubella monoclonal antibodies and viral antigens in the sewershed.


I want to be clear about why this story matters to me. It was not a public health threat. But it was the first time our system picked up a virus that looks like it came from a lab bench rather than from a person. This means that the same radar built to catch measles and H5N1 can also catch things that don’t belong in nature at all. The tools for engineering biology are advancing fast, and AI is lowering the barriers further. For instance, Anthropic regularly releases reports on


[biosecurity threats](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026#biological-misuse-sep-26) they detected among their user base and stopped.


We should also remember that a naturally emerging pathogen can cross the world in a day.


Whether a signal is natural or engineered, accidental or deliberate, the surveillance question is the same: can you see it early, and can you tell people what it means? That is how we think about biosecurity.


**Our technical vision: three layers**


The World Cup showed us what the whole system needs to look like.


*First, a radar built on metagenomics sequencing.* Wide, agnostic, and affordable enough to run continuously.


*Second, confirmatory lab testing for anomalies.* Sequencing tells you something unusual is there. Additional laboratory genotyping via targeted PCR or amplicon sequencing may be needed to confirm if the pathogen is likely derived from infected individuals or from biotech research. Rubella taught us this directly. All our evidence pointed to a biotech source, but without a validated wastewater PCR assay for rubella, we could not close the loop the way we wanted to. The radar should find the anomaly, and a targeted test should confirm it. We are building toward that workflow.


*Third, notification and response with local public health departments.* This is the layer I most underestimated going in. Our average time to report a concerning detection to a partner was under 12 hours. But speed isn’t the same as usefulness. Health departments asked us hard questions. How confident should they be in a result at low concentration? What does a positive mean? How should they communicate uncertainty to the public? What do metrics like genome coverage and minimum reads mean for their decisions?


The metagenomics technology is working and getting better, but the response infrastructure is where we need to invest more. The burden should not fall on health departments to solve this alone. We don’t want to hand over a large dataset and walk away.


Fig. 3 Biobot’s vision for implementation of wastewater metagenomics to enable public health action nationally.


**What happens when 14 becomes 100 or more?**


Fourteen sites were enough to catch measles, resolve mpox to the clade level, and flag a likely biotech derived rubella strain. So I keep asking what happens if we activate metagenomics screening across 100 sites or more in the Biobot Network?


We would have more chances to catch an introduction, whether it arrives from a plane, a farm, or a lab.


**We would know what normal looks like for each community, which makes anything unusual stand out fast.** And we would reach places that have little surveillance today, where a surprise often hurts the most.


It would also pressure test the layers we are still building. At that scale, confirmatory PCR and notification have to work as a real partnership with hundreds of local health departments. A radar that lights up without a plan for what comes next is just a more expensive way to be worried.


Last summer we asked whether we could capture pathogens that came with the crowds. After ten weeks, 579 samples, and one strange rubella signal, my answer is yes. The harder question is whether public health is ready to adopt widescale metagenomics testing. Starting in January, as we welcome our metagenomics program back across our national, ever expanding network, we begin answering that for real.


If you work in public health, run a treatment plant, or have a hard question about how this should work, write to us at epi@biobot.io. We are building this with you.
